**On Keeping Something Alive**

There are sourdough starters in San Francisco said to be over a century old. Nobody can prove the lineage, of course. The yeast and bacteria in a jar today are not the same organisms that lived there in 1900; they are descendants many thousands of generations removed. And yet people speak of these starters the way one might speak of an heirloom clock or a family name, something handed down and continuous.

I find this strange and moving. A starter is not really a thing. It is a process, a relationship between flour, water, time, and someone willing to show up. Neglect it for a few weeks and it sours into gray liquid. Feed it, and it rises again, bubbling and alive, smelling faintly of apples and vinegar.

Most of what matters seems to work this way. A language survives only if someone speaks it tomorrow. A friendship is less a fact than a series of small returns: the text sent, the call made, the question remembered. Even a self is arguably a kind of starter, with cells replaced, opinions revised, the old material quietly exchanged for new while something recognizable persists.

We tend to imagine permanence as stone: monuments, foundations, things that resist change. But perhaps the more durable form of permanence is the living one, the thing that lasts precisely because it keeps changing, because someone keeps tending it.

A jar on a counter. A handful of flour. A little water. Again tomorrow.
